claim: The outer-membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is critical for surface adhesion, pathogenicity, antibiotic resistance and survival.
source: The outer-membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is critical for surface adhesion, pathogenicity, antibiotic resistance and survival.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the importance of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: Hydrophobic β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) are the major constituent of the outer-membrane.
source: The major constituent – hydrophobic β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) – are first secreted across the inner-membrane through the Sec-translocon for delivery to periplasmic chaperones
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the outer membrane.

claim: OMPs are first secreted across the inner-membrane through the Sec-translocon.
source: The major constituent – hydrophobic β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) – are first secreted across the inner-membrane through the Sec-translocon for delivery to periplasmic chaperones
evidence: This is established knowledge about OMP biogenesis pathway.

claim: SurA is a periplasmic chaperone that prevents aggregation of OMPs.
source: The major constituent – hydrophobic β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) – are first secreted across the inner-membrane through the Sec-translocon for delivery to periplasmic chaperones, for example SurA, which prevent aggregation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of SurA.

claim: OMPs are offloaded to the β-Barrel Assembly Machinery (BAM) in the outer-membrane for insertion and folding.
source: OMPs are then offloaded to the β-Barrel Assembly Machinery (BAM) in the outer-membrane for insertion and folding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about OMP biogenesis.

claim: The Holo-TransLocon (HTL) is an assembly of the protein-channel core-complex SecYEG, the ancillary sub-complex SecDF, and the membrane 'insertase' YidC.
source: We show the Holo-TransLocon (HTL) – an assembly of the protein-channel core-complex SecYEG, the ancillary sub-complex SecDF, and the membrane 'insertase' YidC – contacts BAM through periplasmic domains of SecDF and YidC
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors and supported by their experimental data.

claim: HTL contacts BAM through periplasmic domains of SecDF and YidC.
source: We show the Holo-TransLocon (HTL) – an assembly of the protein-channel core-complex SecYEG, the ancillary sub-complex SecDF, and the membrane 'insertase' YidC – contacts BAM through periplasmic domains of SecDF and YidC, ensuring efficient OMP maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by co-immunoprecipitation, EM, and XL-MS data.

claim: The HTL-BAM interaction ensures efficient OMP maturation.
source: We show the Holo-TransLocon (HTL) – an assembly of the protein-channel core-complex SecYEG, the ancillary sub-complex SecDF, and the membrane 'insertase' YidC – contacts BAM through periplasmic domains of SecDF and YidC, ensuring efficient OMP maturation.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays showing accumulation of unfolded OmpA when the interaction is disrupted.

claim: The proton-motive force (PMF) across the inner-membrane acts at distinct stages of protein secretion.
source: Furthermore, the proton-motive force (PMF) across the inner-membrane acts at distinct stages of protein secretion: (1) SecA-driven translocation through SecYEG and (2) communication of conformational changes via SecDF across the periplasm to BAM.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transport assays and functional studies with SecDD519N mutant.

claim: PMF drives SecA-driven translocation through SecYEG.
source: Furthermore, the proton-motive force (PMF) across the inner-membrane acts at distinct stages of protein secretion: (1) SecA-driven translocation through SecYEG
evidence: This is supported by in vitro transport assays and established knowledge.

claim: PMF drives communication of conformational changes via SecDF across the periplasm to BAM.
source: Furthermore, the proton-motive force (PMF) across the inner-membrane acts at distinct stages of protein secretion: (1) SecA-driven translocation through SecYEG and (2) communication of conformational changes via SecDF across the periplasm to BAM.
evidence: This is supported by functional studies with SecDD519N mutant and EM structural analysis.

claim: PMF-driven conformational changes via SecDF drive efficient passage of OMPs.
source: The latter presumably drives efficient passage of OMPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing OmpA maturation defects with SecDD519N.

claim: Precursors of β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) with cleavable N-terminal signal-sequences are targeted to the ubiquitous Sec-machinery.
source: Precursors of β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) with cleavable N-terminal signal-sequences are targeted to the ubiquitous Sec-machinery and driven into the periplasm by the ATPase SecA and the trans-membrane proton-motive force (PMF) (Brundage et al., 1990; Collinson, 2019; Lill et al., 1989; Cranford-Smith and Huber, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: OMPs are driven into the periplasm by the ATPase SecA and the trans-membrane proton-motive force (PMF).
source: Precursors of β-barrel Outer-Membrane Proteins (OMPs) with cleavable N-terminal signal-sequences are targeted to the ubiquitous Sec-machinery and driven into the periplasm by the ATPase SecA and the trans-membrane proton-motive force (PMF) (Brundage et al., 1990; Collinson, 2019; Lill et al., 1989; Cranford-Smith and Huber, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pre-protein signal-sequence is proteolytically cleaved upon completion of translocation.
source: Upon completion, the pre-protein signal-sequence is proteolytically cleaved (Josefsson and Randall, 1981; Chang et al., 1978), releasing the mature unfolded protein into the periplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Signal sequence cleavage releases the mature unfolded protein into the periplasm.
source: Upon completion, the pre-protein signal-sequence is proteolytically cleaved (Josefsson and Randall, 1981; Chang et al., 1978), releasing the mature unfolded protein into the periplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The emergent protein is picked up by periplasmic chaperones, such as SurA and Skp, which prevent aggregation.
source: The emergent protein is then picked up by periplasmic chaperones, such as SurA and Skp, which prevent aggregation (McMorran et al., 2013; Sklar et al., 2007), and somehow facilitate delivery to the β-Barrel Assembly Machinery (BAM) for outer-membrane insertion and folding (Voulhoux et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Periplasmic chaperones facilitate delivery to BAM for outer-membrane insertion and folding.
source: The emergent protein is then picked up by periplasmic chaperones, such as SurA and Skp, which prevent aggregation (McMorran et al., 2013; Sklar et al., 2007), and somehow facilitate delivery to the β-Barrel Assembly Machinery (BAM) for outer-membrane insertion and folding (Voulhoux et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Escherichia coli, BAM consists of a membrane protein complex of subunits BamA-E.
source: In Escherichia coli, BAM consists of a membrane protein complex of subunits BamA-E, of known structure (Bakelar et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2016; Iadanza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The structure of BAM is known.
source: In Escherichia coli, BAM consists of a membrane protein complex of subunits BamA-E, of known structure (Bakelar et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2016; Iadanza et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: BamA is a 16 stranded β-barrel integral membrane protein.
source: The core component, BamA, is a 16 stranded β-barrel integral membrane protein, which projects a large periplasmic stretch of 5 POlypeptide TRanslocation-Associated (POTRA) domains into the periplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BamA structure.

claim: BamA projects a large periplasmic stretch of 5 POTRA domains into the periplasm.
source: The core component, BamA, is a 16 stranded β-barrel integral membrane protein, which projects a large periplasmic stretch of 5 POlypeptide TRanslocation-Associated (POTRA) domains into the periplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BamA structure.

claim: BamB-E are peripheral membrane lipoproteins anchored to the inner leaflet of the outer membrane.
source: BamB-E are peripheral membrane lipoproteins anchored to the inner leaflet of the OM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BAM complex composition.

claim: The mechanism for BAM-facilitated OMP insertion is unknown.
source: In spite of the structural insights, the mechanism for BAM-facilitated OMP insertion is unknown (Ricci and Silhavy, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Complexes spanning both membranes are critical for efficient delivery through many specialised secretion systems.
source: The bacterial periplasm is a challenging environment for unfolded proteins, so complexes spanning both membranes are critical for efficient delivery through many specialised secretion systems (Green and Mecsas, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The core-translocon SecYEG does not possess periplasmic domains of sufficient size to mediate interaction with BAM.
source: The core-translocon, SecYEG, does not possess periplasmic domains of sufficient size to mediate such an interaction (Van den Berg et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of SecYEG supported by citation.

claim: The Holo-TransLocon (HTL) contains the ancillary sub-complex SecDF and the membrane protein 'insertase' YidC.
source: However, the Holo-TransLocon (HTL) contains the ancillary sub-complex SecDF and the membrane protein 'insertase' YidC (Duong and Wickner, 1997; Schulze et al., 2014), both of which contain periplasmic extensions potentially large enough to reach the POTRA domains of BamA.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SecDF and YidC contain periplasmic extensions potentially large enough to reach the POTRA domains of BamA.
source: However, the Holo-TransLocon (HTL) contains the ancillary sub-complex SecDF and the membrane protein 'insertase' YidC (Duong and Wickner, 1997; Schulze et al., 2014), both of which contain periplasmic extensions potentially large enough to reach the POTRA domains of BamA.
evidence: This is inferred from structural knowledge of these proteins.

claim: SecDF is a member of the root nodulation division (RND) superfamily of PMF-driven transporters.
source: SecDF is a member of the so-called root nodulation division (RND) superfamily of PMF-driven transporters (reviewed in Tseng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SecDF is a highly conserved component of the bacterial Sec translocon.
source: It is a highly conserved component of the bacterial Sec translocon, wherein it has long been known to facilitate protein secretion (Duong and Wickner, 1997; Economou et al., 1995; Pogliano and Beckwith, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SecDF has long been known to facilitate protein secretion.
source: It is a highly conserved component of the bacterial Sec translocon, wherein it has long been known to facilitate protein secretion (Duong and Wickner, 1997; Economou et al., 1995; Pogliano and Beckwith, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YidC is essential for membrane protein insertion and thus indispensable.
source: While fellow component of the HTL – YidC – is essential for membrane protein insertion, and thus indispensable (Samuelson et al., 2000; Scotti et al., 2000), mutants of secD and secF are not fatal but severely compromised and cold-sensitive (Gardel et al., 1987), presumably due to deficiencies in envelope biogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutants of secD and secF are not fatal but severely compromised and cold-sensitive.
source: While fellow component of the HTL – YidC – is essential for membrane protein insertion, and thus indispensable (Samuelson et al., 2000; Scotti et al., 2000), mutants of secD and secF are not fatal but severely compromised and cold-sensitive (Gardel et al., 1987), presumably due to deficiencies in envelope biogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The cold-sensitivity of secD and secF mutants is presumably due to deficiencies in envelope biogenesis.
source: While fellow component of the HTL – YidC – is essential for membrane protein insertion, and thus indispensable (Samuelson et al., 2000; Scotti et al., 2000), mutants of secD and secF are not fatal but severely compromised and cold-sensitive (Gardel et al., 1987), presumably due to deficiencies in envelope biogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phenotype.

claim: SecDF confers PMF stimulation of protein secretion.
source: In keeping with other members of the RND family, like AcrB (Eicher et al., 2014), SecDF confers PMF stimulation of protein secretion (Arkowitz and Wickner, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Different structures of SecDF show the large periplasmic domains in different conformational states.
source: Different structures of SecDF show the large periplasmic domains in different conformational states (Furukawa et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2014; Tsukazaki et al., 2011), affected by altering a key residue of the proton transport pathway (SecDD519N – E. coli numbering) (Furukawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Conformational states of SecDF are affected by altering a key residue of the proton transport pathway (SecDD519N).
source: Different structures of SecDF show the large periplasmic domains in different conformational states (Furukawa et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2014; Tsukazaki et al., 2011), affected by altering a key residue of the proton transport pathway (SecDD519N – E. coli numbering) (Furukawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A mechanism has been proposed whereby PMF-driven conformational changes pick up and pull polypeptides as they emerge from the protein-channel exit site of SecY.
source: On this basis, an elaborate mechanism has been proposed whereby PMF-driven conformational changes, at the outer surface of the inner-membrane, pick up and pull polypeptides as they emerge from the protein-channel exit site of SecY.
evidence: This refers to a proposed mechanism in the literature based on structural studies.

claim: ATP- and PMF-driven translocation across the inner-membrane does not require SecDF or YidC; SecYEG and SecA will suffice.
source: Yet, ATP- and PMF-driven translocation across the inner-membrane does not require SecDF or YidC; SecYEG and SecA will suffice (Brundage et al., 1990; Schulze et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There are two PMF-dependent components of protein secretion: an early stage dependent only on SecYEG/SecA and another later event regulated by an AcrB-like SecDF activity.
source: Evidently then, there must be two PMF-dependent components of protein secretion: an early stage dependent only on SecYEG/SecA and another later event regulated by an AcrB-like SecDF activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of established knowledge and the authors' reasoning.

claim: The distinction between two PMF-dependent components of protein secretion has not been fully appreciated.
source: This distinction has not been fully appreciated.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the state of the field.

claim: SecY is present in the lighter inner-membrane fractions in sucrose gradient centrifugation.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis and staining for total protein revealed the presence of SecY in the lighter inner-membrane fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, yellow asterisk – left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: OmpC and OmpF are highly expressed outer-membrane residents.
source: Heating the fractions (required to unfold outer-membrane proteins) prior to SDS-PAGE helped reveal the location of the most highly expressed outer-membrane residents (OmpC and OmpF; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, yellow asterisk – right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: In sucrose gradients, fractions 1–2 mostly contain outer-membranes, and fractions 4–5 are composed mainly of inner-membranes.
source: Thus, in these gradients fractions 1–2 mostly contain outer-membranes, and fractions 4–5 are composed mainly of inner-membranes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing protein distributions.

claim: When over-produced as part of HTL, SecY and SecE show a marked shift of their migration peak towards the outer-membrane containing fractions.
source: However, when over-produced as part of HTL, there is a marked shift of their migration peak towards the outer-membrane containing fractions (Figure 1b, HTL↑).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Over-production of SecDF alone results in SecD, SecY, and SecG migrating into the outer-membrane containing fractions.
source: Interestingly, the over-production of SecDF alone results in a similar effect (Figure 1c), where SecD, SecY, and SecG all migrate into the outer-membrane containing fractions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The migration shift effect is lost when the periplasmic domain of SecD (P1) is removed.
source: An effect which was lost in comparable experiments where the periplasmic domain of SecD (P1) had been removed (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: An interaction between the Sec and Bam complexes, requiring at least the periplasmic domains of SecD, causes an association of inner- and outer-membrane vesicles reflected in the migration shift.
source: Our interpretation of these experiments is that an interaction between the Sec and Bam complexes, requiring at least the periplasmic domains of SecD (and most likely SecF and YidC), causes an association of inner- and outer-membrane vesicles reflected in the shift we observe.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental data.

claim: SecG and SecD of HTL co-immunoprecipitated when pulling with SecG antibody.
source: As expected, SecG (positive control) and SecD of HTL co-immuno-precipitated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: BamA co-immunoprecipitated with SecG.
source: Crucially, BamA could also be detected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Non-specific binding in the immunoprecipitation was either undetectable or considerably lower than the specific co-immuno-precipitant.
source: The specificity of the association was demonstrated by controls omitting the SecG antibody or the SecG protein (produced from membranes extracts of a ΔsecG strain; Nishiyama et al., 1994), wherein non-specific binding was either undetectable, or considerably lower than the specific co-immuno-precipitant (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental controls shown in the figure.

claim: When BAM was over-produced, the yield of BamA recovered in the IPs increased accordingly.
source: When BAM was over-produced the yield of BamA recovered in the IPs increased accordingly (Figure 1d,e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: BamA co-purified with additional components of the BAM complex (BamB and BamD) and with SecD and SecG of the HTL.
source: Western blots showed that BamA co-purified, as expected, with additional components of the BAM complex (BamB and BamD), and crucially also with SecD and SecG of the HTL (Figure 1f; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The phospholipid cardiolipin (CL) is intimately associated with energy-transducing systems, including the Sec-machinery, for both complex stabilisation and efficient transport.
source: The phospholipid cardiolipin (CL) is known to be intimately associated with energy-transducing systems, including the Sec-machinery, for both complex stabilisation and efficient transport (Schulze et al., 2014; Corey et al., 2018; Gold et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: On omission of CL, the interactions of SecG with SecD and BamA were reduced approximately three- and fivefold, respectively.
source: On omission of CL, the interactions of SecG with SecD and BamA were reduced approximately three- and fivefold, respectively (Figure 1d,e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CL stabilises HTL.
source: This lipid-mediated enhancement of the SecG-SecD interaction is consistent with our previous finding that CL stabilises HTL (Schulze et al., 2014) and shows it also holds true for the HTL-BAM interaction.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: CL enhances the HTL-BAM interaction.
source: This lipid-mediated enhancement of the SecG-SecD interaction is consistent with our previous finding that CL stabilises HTL (Schulze et al., 2014) and shows it also holds true for the HTL-BAM interaction.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing reduced interaction without CL.

claim: CL has been shown to be associated with the BAM complex.
source: Apropos, CL has been shown to be associated with the BAM complex (Chorev et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: When mixed together, HTL and BAM co-migrated towards higher glycerol concentrations, beyond those attained by the individual complexes.
source: When mixed together, HTL and BAM co-migrated towards higher glycerol concentrations, beyond those attained by the individual complexes (Figure 2a, yellow asterisk) and consistent with the formation of a larger complex due to an interaction between the two.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The co-migration of HTL and BAM is consistent with the formation of a larger complex due to an interaction between the two.
source: When mixed together, HTL and BAM co-migrated towards higher glycerol concentrations, beyond those attained by the individual complexes (Figure 2a, yellow asterisk) and consistent with the formation of a larger complex due to an interaction between the two.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Only a fraction of the HTL and BAM associates, indicating the interaction is not very strong.
source: The interaction is clear but not very strong, wherein only a fraction of the HTL and BAM associates.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing incomplete association.

claim: The low affinity between HTL and BAM is likely due to the required transient nature of the association between the two translocons in vivo.
source: This low affinity is likely due to the required transient nature of the association between the two translocons in vivo, and also because of the complete breakdown of the inner- and outer-membranes by detergent – required for this experiment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations and biological reasoning.

claim: SecDF and YidC, but not SecYEG, interact with BAM.
source: When the experiment was repeated with the individual constituents of HTL: SecDF and YidC, but not SecYEG, were also shown to interact with BAM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–c, yellow asterisks).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The HTL-BAM complex is large enough (~300×250x150 Å) to contain both Sec and BAM machineries.
source: The subsequent single-particle analysis of the cross-linked material (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a, left, black asterisk; Figure 2—source data 1) revealed a remarkable structure large enough (~300×250x150 Å) to contain both Sec and BAM machineries (Iadanza et al., 2016; Botte et al., 2016), and with a height sufficient to straddle the space between the two membranes (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 3b), especially when considering the plasticity of the periplasm (Zuber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by EM structural data.

claim: The HTL-BAM complex has a height sufficient to straddle the space between the two membranes.
source: The subsequent single-particle analysis of the cross-linked material (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a, left, black asterisk; Figure 2—source data 1) revealed a remarkable structure large enough (~300×250x150 Å) to contain both Sec and BAM machineries (Iadanza et al., 2016; Botte et al., 2016), and with a height sufficient to straddle the space between the two membranes (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 3b), especially when considering the plasticity of the periplasm (Zuber et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by EM structural data and cited knowledge about periplasm dimensions.

claim: Regions of SecDF and the POTRA domains of BamA extend ~60 Å and ~110 Å respectively, sufficient to bridge the gap between membranes.
source: Indeed, regions of SecDF and the POTRA domains of BamA have been shown to extend ~60 Å (Furukawa et al., 2017) and ~110 Å (Ma et al., 2019) respectively, sufficient to bridge this gap.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The locations of YidC, SecDF, and SecYEG were revealed by difference analysis of 3D reconstructions of different sub-complexes.
source: To assign the locations and orientations of the individual constituents of HTL and BAM, we compared the 3D reconstructions of different sub-complexes: BAM bound to SecYEG-DF (without YidC) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c) or SecDF alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 3d). The difference analysis revealed the locations of YidC (Figure 2b, pink; Figure 2—figure supplement 3c, pink arrow), SecDF (Figure 2b, green; Figure 2—figure supplement 3d, green arrow), and SecYEG (Figure 2b, blue; Figure 2—figure supplement 3d, blue arrow) at the bottom of the assembly (assigned as the inner-membrane region).
evidence: This is supported by EM structural analysis.

claim: The orientation of BAM relative to SecDF is different in SecDF-BAM compared to HTL-BAM.
source: The orientation of BAM relative to SecDF is different in SecDF-BAM compared to HTL-BAM (Figure 2—figure supplement 3d, red arrows), possibly due to its known ability to move (see below), and/or the absence of stabilising interactions with the missing HTL components (SecYEG and YidC).
evidence: This is observed in the EM structures and interpreted by the authors.

claim: Removing BamB from the complex results in the loss of significant mass in the area designated as the outer-membrane region.
source: Removing BamB from the complex results in the loss of significant mass in the area designated as the outer-membrane region (Figure 2b, orange; Figure 2—figure supplement 3e, orange arrow).
evidence: This is supported by EM structural analysis.

claim: The complex lacking BamB shows a diminishment of the density assigned as YidC, suggestive of a mutual interaction between the two.
source: Interestingly, the complex lacking BamB shows a diminishment of the density assigned as YidC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3e, pink arrow), suggestive of a mutual interaction between the two.
evidence: This is inferred from the EM structural data.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of the HTL-BAM complex was produced with an overall resolution of 18.2 Å.
source: Despite heterogeneity in the sample, we were able to isolate a cross-linked HTL-BAM complex by size exclusion chromatography and produce a low-resolution cryo-EM structure (Figure 2c; Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Figure 2—figure supplement 5a (a similar fraction was used to that marked by the black asterisk) and Figure 2—source data 1) with an overall resolution of 18.2 Å.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: The cryo-EM structure reveals the basic architecture of the HTL-BAM assembly and the arrangement of constituent subunits.
source: Taken together with the difference map generated by negative stain-EM (Figure 2b; Figure 2—figure supplement 3), the structure reveals the basic architecture of the assembly and the arrangement of constituent subunits.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM and negative stain EM data.

claim: The periplasmic domains of SecD, YidC, and to a lesser degree SecF, extend to establish multiple interactions with the BAM lipoproteins.
source: In this respect, it is interesting to note in the structure that the periplasmic domains of SecD, YidC, and to a lesser degree SecF, extend to establish multiple interactions with the BAM lipoproteins suggesting a pivotal role for these subunits in the formation of the HTL-BAM complex (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is observed in the EM structures.

claim: The bridge between HTL and BAM helps to define a very large cavity between the inner- and outer-membrane regions.
source: This bridge between the two complexes also helps to define a very large cavity between the inner- and outer-membrane regions (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is observed in the EM structures.

claim: BamB can be unambiguously docked into the cryo-EM structure.
source: Some components of the BAM complex, such as BamB, can be unambiguoulsy docked into the cryo-EM structure (Figure 2c), localised by negative stain difference mapping (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 3e), and its recognisable β-propeller shape (Bakelar et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the EM data and known structure of BamB.

claim: The locations of BamA, BamC, and BamD are suggested according to the cryo-EM density and the constraints of the XL-MS data.
source: We also suggest the locations of BamA, BamC, and BamD according to the cryo-EM density and the constraints of the XL-MS data (Figure 2e; Figure 2—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This is based on integration of cryo-EM and XL-MS data.

claim: The inner-membrane region of the HTL bound to BAM is much more open than the previous structure of the isolated version.
source: The inner-membrane region of the HTL – while bound to BAM – is much more open than the previous structure of the isolated version (Botte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the new structure with the previously published structure.

claim: In the new open structure, the locations of SecYEG, SecDF, and YidC can be easily distinguished.
source: In the new open structure, the locations of the core-complex SecYEG, SecDF, and YidC can be easily distinguished, in which the former two are connected within the membrane by two bridges (Figure 2f, left).
evidence: This is observed in the EM structure.

claim: The connections between SecYEG and SecDF could be the binding sites of CL and the central lipid pool.
source: These connections could be the binding sites of CL and the central lipid pool identified previously, required for structural stability and translocon activity (Schulze et al., 2014; Corey et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structure and previous knowledge.

claim: Within SecYEG, the protein-channel can be visualised through the centre, along with the lateral gate.
source: Within SecYEG, the protein-channel can be visualised through the centre, along with the lateral gate (LG, required for signal sequence binding and inner-membrane protein insertion) facing towards SecDF, YidC, and the putative central lipid pool (Martin et al., 2019; Figure 2f, right).
evidence: This is observed in the EM structure.

claim: The HTL bound to BAM seems to be more open when compared to the previously published low-resolution cryo-EM structure.
source: As mentioned above, the HTL bound to BAM in our EM structure (Figure 3, structure ii) seems to be more open when compared to the previously published low-resolution cryo-EM structure (Botte et al., 2016) (emd3056; Figure 3, structure i) and also displays a more prominent periplasmic region.
evidence: This is observed by comparing structures.

claim: Preparations of HTL alone contain both a 'compact' state and a proportion of an 'open' state.
source: Preparations of HTL alone, made in this study, contain both a 'compact' state (Figure 3, structure iii) similar to that of the previously published structure (Figure 3, structure i), as well as a proportion of an 'open' state, with proud periplasmic domains, not previously described (Figure 3, structure iv) and apparently more similar to that seen in the HTL-BAM structure (Figure 3, structure ii).
evidence: This is observed in the EM data from this study.

claim: The HTL sample used is extremely pure, of known subunit composition and not prone to oligomerisation.
source: The HTL sample used here is extremely pure, of known subunit composition and not prone to oligomerisation (Schulze et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on previous characterization of the HTL preparation.

claim: The larger 'open' form of HTL is not due to the presence of contaminants, unknown additional partner proteins, or dimerisation.
source: So, we can rule out that this larger form, assigned as an 'open' state, of HTL is not due to the presence of contaminants, unknown additional partner proteins, or dimerisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the purity and characterization of the sample.

claim: Lipid content within the HTL is critical for proper structure and function.
source: Lipid content within the HTL is critical for proper structure and function, and CL is particularly important for protein translocation through the Sec machinery (Schulze et al., 2014; Corey et al., 2018; Gold et al., 2010; Hendrick and Wickner, 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The presence of different populations of HTL – 'compact' and 'open' states – is likely due to varying interactions with lipids, including CL.
source: Therefore, the reason for the presence of these different populations of the HTL – 'compact' and 'open' states – is likely due to varying interactions with lipids, including CL.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known importance of lipids for HTL structure.

claim: Augmenting the HTL with CL during purification increased the proportion of the 'open' state from 8% to 17%.
source: In line with this hypothesis, augmenting the HTL with CL during purification increased the proportion of the 'open' state (from 8% to 17%), which could be enriched by glycerol gradient fractionation (to 32%), and further stabilised by cross-linking (to 40%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The open conformation is the state capable of interacting with the BAM complex.
source: Evidently then, it seems likely that the open conformation (Figure 3, structure iv) is the state capable of interacting with the BAM complex (Figure 3, structure ii).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity and the CL-dependence of both the open state and the HTL-BAM interaction.

claim: The 'open' structure and the 'compact' structure may reflect different functional states of the translocon.
source: The 'open' structure, and the 'compact' structure seen before (Botte et al., 2016), may reflect different functional states of the translocon.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: The dimensions of the HTL-BAM structure are sufficient to span roughly the distance between the inner- and outer-membranes.
source: The dimensions of the HTL-BAM structure are sufficient to span roughly the distance between the inner- and outer-membranes, but only just.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural dimensions and known periplasm width.

claim: Increasing the thickness of the periplasm might be expected to stymie formation of HTL-BAM complexes.
source: Thus, increasing the thickness of the periplasm might therefore be expected to stymie formation of HTL-BAM complexes, as previously observed for other trans-periplasmic complexes (Asmar et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural dimensions and cited precedent.

claim: Increasing the length of lpp increases the width of the periplasm from ~250 Å for wild type lpp to ~290 Å when an additional 21 residues are added (Lpp+21).
source: Increasing the length of lpp increases the width of the periplasm, from ~250 Å for wild type lpp to ~290 Å when an additional 21 residues are added to the resultant protein (Lpp+21) (Asmar et al., 2017; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: When the inter-membrane distance was increased, the integrity of the HTL in the inner-membrane was unaffected.
source: Consistent with our model, when the inter-membrane distance was increased, the integrity of the HTL in the inner-membrane was unaffected, but the recovery of HTL-BAM was reduced more than threefold (Figure 4b,c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: When the inter-membrane distance was increased, the recovery of HTL-BAM was reduced more than threefold.
source: Consistent with our model, when the inter-membrane distance was increased, the integrity of the HTL in the inner-membrane was unaffected, but the recovery of HTL-BAM was reduced more than threefold (Figure 4b,c; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: secDF null mutants exhibit a severe export defect and are only just viable.
source: secDF null mutants exhibit a severe export defect and are only just viable (Pogliano and Beckwith, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Depletion of SecDF-YajC results in a strong growth defect.
source: Depletion of SecDF-YajC results in a strong growth defect (Figure 5b, panels 1 and 2), which can be rescued by recombinant expression of wild-type secDF (Nouwen and Driessen, 2002; Figure 5b, panels 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The growth defect from SecDF-YajC depletion can be rescued by recombinant expression of wild-type secDF.
source: Depletion of SecDF-YajC results in a strong growth defect (Figure 5b, panels 1 and 2), which can be rescued by recombinant expression of wild-type secDF (Nouwen and Driessen, 2002; Figure 5b, panels 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and cited work.

claim: Expression of secDD519NF, which produces a complex incapable of proton transport, did not complement the growth defect.
source: In contrast, expression of secDD519NF, which results in the production of a complex incapable of proton transport (Furukawa et al., 2017), did not complement the defect (Figure 5b, panels 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Despite the blocked proton pathway through SecDF, there was little difference in the efficiencies of proOmpA transport into IMVs.
source: Both sets of vesicles contained similar concentrations of SecY (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), yet despite the blocked proton pathway through SecDF, there was little difference in the efficiencies of transport (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: SecA mediated ATP- and PMF-driven protein translocation through the inner-membrane via HTL does not require a functional proton wire through SecDF.
source: Most importantly, the results demonstrate that SecA mediated ATP- and PMF-driven protein translocation through the inner-membrane via HTL does not require a functional proton wire through SecDF (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The proton translocating activity of SecD, needed for general secretion and cell survival, must be required for something downstream of protein transport through the inner-membrane.
source: Therefore, the proton translocating activity of SecD, needed for general secretion and cell survival, must be required for something downstream of protein transport through the inner-membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of the growth defect with SecDD519N and the lack of effect on inner membrane transport.

claim: Elevated levels of unfolded OmpA (ufOmpA) in the periplasm are a classical signature of OMP maturation deficiencies.
source: Elevated levels of unfolded OmpA (ufOmpA) in the periplasm are a classical signature of OMP maturation deficiencies (Sklar et al., 2007; Bulieris et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Folded OmpA (fOmpA) does not denature fully in SDS unless boiled; it therefore runs at a lower apparent molecular mass compared to ufOmpA when analysed by SDS-PAGE.
source: It can be easily monitored by SDS-PAGE and western blotting: folded OmpA (fOmpA) does not denature fully in SDS unless boiled; it therefore runs at a lower apparent molecular mass compared to ufOmpA when analysed by SDS-PAGE (Figure 5d, left; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c; Sklar et al., 2007; Bulieris et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and demonstrated in the figures.

claim: Under SecDF depletion conditions, high levels of unfolded OmpA accumulate in the periplasm, particularly during the exponential phase.
source: Under SecDF depletion conditions (Figure 5e, red squares), high levels of unfolded OmpA accumulate in the periplasm, particularly during the exponential phase when the demand for outer-membrane biogenesis is highest (Figure 5d, yellow asterisk; Figure 5f,g; Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Under permissive conditions (arabinose), a more modest increase in ufOmpA is observable after 1.5 hr, but it recovers fully by 3 hr.
source: Meanwhile, under permissive conditions (Figure 5e–g, arabinose, orange circles), a more modest increase in ufOmpA is observable after 1.5 hr, but it recovers fully by 3 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The transient increase in ufOmpA under permissive conditions is accompanied by a transient decrease in SecDF levels.
source: Notably, this change is accompanied by a transient decrease in SecDF levels (Figure 5e, orange circles).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The expression of secDF and levels of ufOmpA in the cell envelope are anti-correlated, exacerbated during fast cell growth.
source: Clearly, the expression of secDF and levels of ufOmpA in the cell envelope are anti-correlated, exacerbated during fast cell growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing inverse relationship.

claim: The effects on ufOmpA were not an indirect consequence of BamA loss, which was unperturbed.
source: These effects were not an indirect consequence of BamA loss, which was unperturbed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Depletion of SecDF reduces the interaction between HTL and BAM, hampering transport of β-barrel proteins to the outer-membrane resulting in a build-up of ufOmpA in the periplasm.
source: Taken together, the data show that depletion of SecDF reduces the interaction between HTL and BAM, and thereby hampers transport of β-barrel proteins to the outer-membrane resulting in a build-up of ufOmpA in the periplasm.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the combined experimental data.

claim: A backlog of unfolded OMP could compromise outer-membrane biogenesis and its integrity, explaining the cold-sensitivity of secDF mutants.
source: A backlog of unfolded OMP could compromise outer-membrane biogenesis and its integrity, and thereby explain the cold-sensitivity of secDF mutants (Gardel et al., 1987).
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: Proton translocation through SecD is crucial for cell growth.
source: Proton translocation through SecD is crucial for cell growth (Figure 5b, panels 5 and 6), but evidently not for PMF-stimulated protein transport through the inner-membrane via SecYEG (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Proton translocation through SecD is not required for PMF-stimulated protein transport through the inner-membrane via SecYEG.
source: Proton translocation through SecD is crucial for cell growth (Figure 5b, panels 5 and 6), but evidently not for PMF-stimulated protein transport through the inner-membrane via SecYEG (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The wild type, but not the mutant SecDD519N, reduced unfolded OmpA in the periplasm to levels much closer to that of the strain grown in permissive conditions.
source: The subsequent analysis showed the wild type, but not the mutant, reduced unfolded OmpA in the periplasm to levels much closer to that of the strain grown in permissive conditions (Figure 5g; green and purple, respectively; Figure 5—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Proton transport through SecD is required for efficient outer-membrane protein folding.
source: Therefore, proton transport through SecD is apparently required for efficient outer-membrane protein folding.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing ufOmpA accumulation with SecDD519N.

claim: The defective variant SecDD519NF still interacts with BAM.
source: To confirm the defective variant SecDD519NF still interacts with BAM, we repeated co-IP experiments as before (Figure 1d,e) using membrane extracts derived from the SecDF depletion strains grown in the non-permissive condition (glucose; Figure 5b), but complemented with plasmids driving the expression of the wild type or mutant secDF, or nothing at all (empty plasmid).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experimental data.

claim: The levels of co-immuno-precipitated SecG, SecD, and BamA were the same irrespective of complementation with the wild type or mutant forms of secDF.
source: The levels of co-immuno-precipitated SecG, SecD, and BamA were the same irrespective of complementation with the wild type or mutant forms of secDF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-IPs.

claim: The integrity of the HTL and its ability to interact with the BAM complex do not require a functional proton wire through SecD.
source: Evidently then, the integrity of the HTL and its ability to interact with the BAM complex do not require a functional proton wire through SecD.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing similar interactions with wild type and mutant SecDF.

claim: The mutant SecDD519N's compromised OmpA maturation must be due to the loss of proton flow through SecD, rather than a loss of contact between HTL and BAM.
source: Therefore, the mutant's compromised OmpA maturation must be due to the loss of proton flow through SecD, rather than a loss of contact between HTL and BAM.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of functional and interaction data.

claim: The 2D classification of HTL-SecDD519N shows the open state is populated to a similar extent compared to the unmodified HTL.
source: The 2D classification of HTL-SecDD519N shows the open state is populated to a similar extent compared to the unmodified HTL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in the figure.

claim: Blocking the proton pathway in SecD results in a shorter extension of the periplasmic domains of the HTL, compared to the native version.
source: However, the 'open' states are significantly different: blocking the proton pathway in SecD results in a shorter extension of the periplasmic domains of the HTL, compared to the native version (Figure 6, structures ii versus v).
evidence: This is supported by EM structural data shown in the figure.

claim: The conformational difference in HTL with SecDD519N is consistent with the conformational change observed at atomic resolution in SecDF alone.
source: This is consistent with the conformational change observed at atomic resolution in SecDF alone (Figure 6, structures iii versus vi) (Furukawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published atomic structures.

claim: PMF-dependent conformational changes of SecD would be communicated to the outer-membrane.
source: Even at the current low-resolution description of the HTL-BAM complex (Figure 2), it is clear that these observed PMF-dependent conformational changes of SecD would be communicated to the outer-membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing the connection between SecD and BAM.

claim: Direct contact between HTL and BAM is required for efficient OMP biogenesis in rapidly growing cells.
source: Evidently, direct contact between HTL and BAM is required for efficient OMP biogenesis in rapidly growing cells.
evidence: This is supported by the functional data showing ufOmpA accumulation when the interaction is disrupted.

claim: The interaction between HTL and BAM could enable large protein fluxes to stream through the periplasm, while minimising aggregation and proteolysis.
source: The interaction could enable large protein fluxes to stream through the periplasm, while minimising aggregation and proteolysis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The presence of super-complexes that bridge both membranes appears to be a fundamental feature of the Gram negative bacterial cell envelope.
source: The presence of super-complexes that bridge both membranes appears to be a fundamental feature of the Gram negative bacterial cell envelope – critical for a whole range of activities including the export of proteins through a gamut of different secretion systems (e.g. type I, II, III, IV, and VI) (Green and Mecsas, 2016); now including the Sec machinery.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the current findings and cited knowledge.

claim: The HTL encloses a lipid-containing cavity within the membrane, presumably to facilitate membrane protein insertion.
source: It has already been shown that the HTL encloses a lipid-containing cavity within the membrane, presumably to facilitate membrane protein insertion (Botte et al., 2016; Martin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the super-complex between HTL and BAM there is a much larger extension of the cavity opening into the periplasm.
source: Remarkably, in the super-complex between HTL and BAM there is a much larger extension of this cavity opening into the periplasm (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the EM structure.

claim: The cavity in the HTL-BAM complex would seem an obvious place for OMP passage and for the interaction with chaperones.
source: This would seem an obvious place for OMP passage and for the interaction with chaperones (Figure 7) and is of sufficient size to do so.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: SurA is known to interact with BamA.
source: SurA is known to interact with BamA (Sklar et al., 2007), and an interaction with the HTL also seems likely (Figure 7).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation, and speculation about HTL interaction.

claim: YfgM and PpiD are thought to mediate interactions between emergent periplasmic proteins and chaperones.
source: Other ancillary factors of the Sec machinery have also been implicated: YfgM and PpiD are thought to mediate interactions between emergent periplasmic proteins and chaperones (Götzke et al., 2014); indeed, PpiD has also been shown to interact with SecYEG and YidC (Jauss et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: yfgL and yfgM are in the same operon, the former encoding a subunit of the BAM complex (BamB).
source: Interestingly, yfgL and yfgM are in the same operon (Blattner et al., 1997), the former encoding a subunit of the BAM complex (BamB) (Wu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A recent proteomic analysis identifies cross-membrane interactions involving SecYEG, BAM and the chaperones YfgM and PpiD.
source: Moreover, a recent proteomic analysis of the E. coli 'membrane protein interactome' identifies cross-membrane interactions involving SecYEG, BAM and the chaperones YfgM and PpiD (Carlson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The periplasmic domain of SecD is central to the physical HTL-BAM interaction.
source: From our data it is clear that the periplasmic domain of SecD is central to the physical HTL-BAM interaction.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing loss of interaction when P1 is deleted.

claim: The non-functioning SecDF is fully capable of conferring an interaction with BAM but is presumably unable to transmit PMF-dependent conformational changes relayed from the inner-membrane.
source: Even more intriguing though is the requirement for a functioning proton wire through the SecDF trans-membrane domain. The non-functioning SecDF is fully capable of conferring an interaction with BAM but is presumably unable to transmit PMF-dependent conformational changes relayed from the inner-membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP and functional data with SecDD519N.

claim: The static interaction of HTL and BAM is insufficient to enable efficient OMP maturation.
source: This static interaction of HTL and BAM is insuffient to enable efficient OMP maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing ufOmpA accumulation with SecDD519N.

claim: The consequences of preventing PMF inducing dynamic interplay between HTL and BAM are as severe as the disconnection induced by SecDF depletion.
source: The consequences of preventing PMF inducing dynamic interplay between HTL and BAM are as severe as the disconnection induced by SecDF depletion.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the functional effects of SecDF depletion and SecDD519N mutation.

claim: The requirement for PMF-driven inter-membrane dynamic connectivity raises the prospect of TonB-style energy-coupling from the inner-membrane for OMP folding and insertion at the outer-membrane.
source: The requirement for PMF-driven inter-membrane dynamic connectivity raises the intriguing prospect of TonB-style energy-coupling from the inner-membrane (Celia et al., 2016): that is the transmission of free energy available from the PMF via the Sec-machinery (Brundage et al., 1990; Arkowitz and Wickner, 1994; Schiebel et al., 1991) for OMP folding and insertion at the outer-membrane.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and analogy to TonB.

claim: One of the primary roles of SecDF is in inter-membrane trafficking and energy transduction.
source: We therefore propose that one of the primary roles of SecDF is in inter-membrane trafficking and energy transduction.
evidence: This is the authors' proposal based on their experimental findings.

claim: There are two distinct requirements of the PMF in protein secretion: one for SecA-driven translocation through SecYEG at the inner-membrane, and another for late stages of OMP maturation.
source: Thus, there appears to be two distinct requirements of the PMF in protein secretion: one for the early stage – SecA-driven translocation through SecYEG at the inner-membrane, and another for late stages of OMP maturation.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on their experimental findings.

claim: An 'open' state of the HTL interacts with the BAM complex.
source: Here, we show that an 'open' state of the HTL interacts with the BAM complex, and that the periplasmic regions of SecD can adopt different conformations, reminiscent of those previously characterised as the I- and F-forms (Furukawa et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by the EM structural data.

claim: When a key proton carrying residue of the inner-membrane segment of the translocon is neutralised (SecDD519N), the periplasmic domain adopts the F-form.
source: when a key proton carrying residue of the inner-membrane segment of the translocon is neutralised – SecDD519N – the periplasmic domain adopts the F-form (Furukawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and observed in the EM data.

claim: Successive protonation and deprotonation result in large, cyclical movements between the I- and F-forms during PMF-driven proton transport from the periplasm to the cytosol.
source: Thus, successive protonation (approximated by SecDD519N) and deprotonation result in large, cyclical movements – between the I- and F-forms – during PMF-driven proton transport from the periplasm to the cytosol (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and established knowledge about proton transport.

claim: The occurrence of conformational changes in SecD while connected to the BAM complex results in long-range energetic coupling between the inner- and outer-membranes.
source: Presumably then, the occurance of these conformational changes, while connected to the BAM complex, results in long-range energetic coupling between the inner- and outer-membranes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Cardiolipin (CL) is important for the stabilisation of the 'open' state of the HTL and its interaction with the BAM machinery.
source: Interestingly, the phospholipid cardiolipin (CL) is important for the stabilisation of the 'open' state of the HTL and its interaction with the BAM machinery.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing CL-dependence of the open state and HTL-BAM interaction.

claim: CL has been shown to be critical for PMF-driven protein translocation through SecYEG.
source: It is probably not a coincidence that this lipid has already been shown to be critical for PMF-driven protein translocation through SecYEG (Corey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Direct association between inner- and outer-membrane components appears to be the rule rather than the exception for transporters embedded in double membrane systems.
source: Direct association between inner- and outer-membrane components appears to be the rule rather than the exception for transporters embedded in double membrane systems: parallels with the translocation assembly module (TAM) for auto-transporter secretion (Selkrig et al., 2012), and the TIC-TOC import machinery of chloroplasts (Chen et al., 2018) are striking, given the respective outer-membrane components (TamA and TOC75) are homologous of BamA.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the current findings and cited examples.

claim: TamA and TOC75 are homologous to BamA.
source: Direct association between inner- and outer-membrane components appears to be the rule rather than the exception for transporters embedded in double membrane systems: parallels with the translocation assembly module (TAM) for auto-transporter secretion (Selkrig et al., 2012), and the TIC-TOC import machinery of chloroplasts (Chen et al., 2018) are striking, given the respective outer-membrane components (TamA and TOC75) are homologous of BamA.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Subunits of the MItochondrial contact site and Cristae Organizing System (MICOS) connect the energy-transducing ATP synthase of the inner-membrane and SAM at the outer-membrane.
source: Indeed, subunits of the MItochondrial contact site and Cristae Organizing System (MICOS) connect the energy-transducing ATP synthase of the inner-membrane and SAM at the outer-membrane (Ott et al., 2015; Rampelt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.
